Hapoel Be'er Sheva Europa League form:.

Hapoel Be'er Sheva form (all competitions):.

Besiktas will be without Umit Akdag, who is suspended for Thursday's encounter, while every other player is available for the Black Eagles.

Junior Olaitan has scored or assisted in all four of his Europa League main-draw appearances for the hosts and could become just the second African player since 2009-10 to achieve that feat in his first five such matches in the competition.

Dusan Vlahovic will hope to continue his rich scoring form after netting a brace against Konyaspor, taking his tally to four goals in his last two matches.

Hapoel Beer-Sheva will be without Eliel Peretz, who has been sidelined since late October with a groin injury, while Dan Biton remains unavailable due to a heart-related problem.

Matan Baltaxa is also a doubt after sustaining a foot injury, while Ofir Marciano is expected to remain sidelined with a calf problem.

Besiktas possible starting lineup:.

Nubel; Murillo, Bulut, Topcu, R Yilmaz; Ndidi; Trossard, Kocku, Olaitan, Fakili; Vlahovic.

Hapoel Be'er Sheva possible starting lineup:.

Marciano; Mizrahi, Vitor, Nachmias, Amador; Amankwah, Yehoshua, Ahmed; East, Zlatanovic, Ganah.

Besiktas possess greater attacking quality and head into this encounter on the back of consecutive domestic victories, while Beer-Sheva's struggles in Europe and their poor away record suggest that the visitors could have a difficult evening in Georgia, with Italiano's side expected to secure a comfortable victory.

It marks a significant step forward from his first season at the Amex Stadium, when he scored twice in 21 Premier League appearances, making just two starts.

Brighton head coach Hurzeler - who last season questioned Kostoulas’ commitment to training - is now impressed by the progress, particularly the forward's growing physical strength, work rate and understanding of the demands of English football.

According to recent reports, but Kostoulas says there has been no dramatic change to his game. Instead, he has gradually learned what the team requires from him and become more comfortable in his role.

"Mainly, it's about understanding what the team wants," he said to Sussex World.

"For me, as a striker, with time and after some months, I started to understand that. With the minutes I've got and things like that, I gained the trust of my teammates and I want to keep going like that.".

Hurzeler has previously highlighted the difference in the youngster's ability to compete physically, saying: "When you see him now and how resilient he is in personal duels, it's something completely different.".

The Brighton boss has also praised his pressing and attitude towards improvement, describing a player who is becoming increasingly professional.

Kostoulas credits the manager's clarity and attention to detail, while revealing he has enjoyed the greater freedom given to him in the attacking role.

"He's clear with the instructions he gives on the pitch. He's always clear," he said.

"But I think I didn't change the way I was playing. Last season I could also do these types of things on the pitch, but I have more of a free role, especially in my position. I like it.".

The transition from Olympiacos to Brighton was not without its challenges, however.

Kostoulas admits the biggest adjustment was the daily routine, with longer hours at the training ground, different training methods and a greater emphasis on meetings and preparation.

Industry observers note that "The daily routine, I think, was the hardest," he told Sussex World. "We spend many hours at the training ground, more than I was used to in Greece.

"There are different types of training, a different approach to the game, more meetings and things like that.".

He was helped by some of Brighton's more experienced players, with former midfielder James Milner playing a particularly key role during his first season.

"Most of the older players would come and say something to me as advice," Kostoulas explained. "Last season, James Milner was speaking a lot to me and trying to help me.".

He still occasionally speaks to Milner, while Pascal Gross has also become an crucial figure in his development.

For Kostoulas, having someone to turn to is vital when moving to a different country and footballing culture.

"It's crucial to have someone to help you understand the way the team works here," he explained to Sussex World.

Sources indicate that "It's totally different. If someone from here moves to Greece, they will also need time. It will be hard for them.

"You have to find someone you can trust, have a good relationship with, speak to and who can give you an understanding of most of the things here and what's expected.".

There is also the prospect of sharing the pitch with fellow Greek forward Stefanos Tsitsimas, whose return from a lengthy spell out has delighted Kostoulas.

Industry observers note that "I'm really happy for him," he mentioned. "He has a really good mindset and I have big trust in him. I think he will do great.".

Kostoulas was keen to avoid looking too far ahead when asked about Brighton's ambitions after their impressive start to the season.

Rather than focus on the possibility of challenging at the top of the table or making a deep run in Europe, he insists the squad are concentrating on the next match.

"We don't think about what will happen after six months when the season will be finished," he remarked to Sussex World.

"We're just enjoying every day, trying to be happy and win as many games as we can.".

#117999. Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s upcoming biology skills wow scientists

Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s upcoming biology skills wow scientists

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Accurately predicting protein structures has been the preserve of specialist AI tools like AlphaFold — but now general-purpose models are catching up.
  • Earlier this month, Xinming Tu set out to test what artificial-intelligence models know about proteins.
  • He left the analysis to run overnight and woke up shocked at the results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Accurately predicting protein structures has been the preserve of specialist AI tools like AlphaFold — but now general-purpose models are catching up. Credit: EMBL-EBI (CC0).

Earlier this month, Xinming Tu set out to test what artificial-intelligence models know about proteins. Tu, a researcher at an AI biology tech giant called Phylo in South San Francisco, California, asked large language models (LLMs) from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google to predict the sequences of obscure bacterial proteins.

He left the analysis to run overnight and woke up shocked at the results. The latest versions of Anthropic’s Claude models had outperformed other LLMs — but also specialized ‘protein language models’, which are trained on vast troves of sequence data and specially designed for such tasks.

Scientists are using AI to dream up revolutionary new proteins.

Scientists are using AI to dream up revolutionary new proteins.

When Tu and Leo Chen, a computational biologist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, shared the results in a 16 November blogpost, it set off a frenzy among computational biologists to see what other protein biology LLMs such as Claude could do. For instance, Tu and Chen and others have found it could perform a key step in protein-structure prediction.

It has been revealed that and on 24 November, OpenAI unveiled that its latest language models had successfully designed upcoming proteins, some of which behaved as expected when made and tested in the lab. The results hint that the latest LLMs might be gaining a sophisticated understanding of protein biology.

The research has kicked off a debate over the future of biological AI. Some scientists predict that ‘general purpose’ models such as Claude and ChatGPT will eventually outperform specialist tools such as AlphaFold at tasks including protein structure prediction and design.

“We want to see a world where a scientist can just describe in natural language what they want a ChatGPT model to do, and the model can just be infinitely flexible and design exactly what the person wants,” says Joy Jiao, who leads life-sciences research at OpenAI in San Francisco, California.

In a recent development, but some researchers question the extent to which LLMs are learning underlying lessons in protein biology. They suggest that some of their abilities could be the result of regurgitating training data.

The release of AlphaFold2, Google DeepMind’s blockbuster protein-structure-prediction AI, in 2020 released a revolution in biological AI. There is now a vast ecosystem of software — much of it open source — for modelling different properties of proteins, such as how they interact with possible drugs, and for designing new proteins.

Recent findings suggest that researchers have begun using LLMs to orchestrate these specialist models, but it has mostly been as a time-saving measure, indicates Martin Pačesa, a structural biologist at the University of Zurich. “In most cases, a specialist will always perform better than a generalist for a given task,” he says.

Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI.

Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI.

To see if an LLM could stand in for specialist protein-design tools, Jiao and her colleagues asked an OpenAI model called GPT-6.2 to design 3D protein structures capable of binding to five different biological targets, including proteins implicated in cancer and immune disorders. After the LLMs generated the designs, the researchers used a specialist AI tool to determine a corresponding genetic sequence. Lab experiments confirmed that around 11% of designs were able to bind their target.

In other experiments, the OpenAI team indicated that its LLMs could design protein sequences, redesign existing antibodies, and other tasks typically performed by specialist tools. In some cases, the LLM performed as well as some specialist tools, and in others, such as predicting the 3D structure of proteins, it was far off. OpenAI researchers describe the work in a blogpost and technical paper.

According to recent reports, jiao emphasizes that the work is a proof of principle, and that specialized AI tools were still needed for key steps. But Masatoshi Uehara, an OpenAI researcher who was part of the effort, believes that LLMs will only get better at protein biology. “I believe the large language model can technically beat every specialized model in even each capability,” he says.

Sometimes the arithmetic scarcely adds up. Saturday afternoon in the sunshine: for sharing eight goals in a lavish celebration of the sport, one point. Tuesday night in temperatures that froze the breath and numbed the fingers: for a routine 3-1 victory: three points.

But Borough's players, management and frozen supporters were not complaining. Steve King's side had played positively, stood up strong against physically powerful opponents, and they got all the unglamorous things right.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

A smart move for 1-0 on 24 minutes, and after an Aveley equaliser, a second goal on the stroke of half-time. And a superb Kai Corbett strike early in the second half to put clear distance between the teams.

Aveley were always chasing the game - and chase it they did - but the Sports deserved their victory, and King's squad now sit third in the division, three points behind leaders Welling but with a game in hand.

Credit, too, to the 529 hardy souls who wrapped themselves in layers of scarves, coats and headgear to enjoy a proper football contest in which the visitors also played their part. Team sport is for sharing - and just a little bit of shared suffering to cheer on your team.

King chose to shuffle the pack a little on for Aveley's visit. Liam Nash, Max Sheaf and Darren McQueen took a rest, and the manager bolstered his midfield with the return of Craig Eastmond. Paul McCallum took a lone striker role - although with ample support from the players around him. Aveley, robust and physically strong, lined up with a proper old-fashioned 4-4-2.

Early stages were quite cagey, but a goalmouth melee on 12 minutes saw Corbett's low effort cleared, and the momentum was with Borough.

Corbett, two-goal hero on Saturday, found Aveley doubling up on him: The Millers' staff had done their homework. And with the industrious visitors defending from the front, as the coaching jargon calls it, the Sports needed to turn possession into scoring chances.

Industry observers note that but the patience and persistence finally brought reward on 24 minutes. Corbett's corner was met first by Elliott Johnson and then McCallum, but with Aveley throwing bodies on the line, both were blocked. But the second block fell invitingly for Freddie Carter, who blasted his shot high into the roof of the net.

In a recent development, aveley had spent much of the first half-hour bravely covering, blocking, spoiling – but the 15 minutes before half-time saw the Essex side pushing forward and suddenly threatening to open up the Sports defence. On 40 minutes they swept through the inside-right channel and a lovely cross from Anthony Jeffery was met by massive striker Matt Johnson for 1-1.

Industry observers note that borough's response was almost immediate: with the Priory Lane scoreboard glowing on 45 minutes, a sweet move into the final third was prompted by Matt Hayden, Eastbourne's gleeful young full-back, who found Terrell Egbri on the right. The bustling winger delivered a lovely cross, met by skipper Josh Rees with an unstoppable diving header to restore the lead.

The second half resumed as the first had left off - or almost. Aveley are a resilient, physical outfit - within the laws and spirit of the game - and they came at Borough with renewed impetus.

Question: would a single goal lead see the Sports survive a whole 45 minutes? Answer: Corbett. From a set-piece, the hero of Enfield slalomed through a ridiculously tight penalty area to deliver a rocket into the top left corner of the Mllers' net.

Recent findings suggest that aveley did have their chances - or at least the promising approach work. But they could not quite find that final piercing pass to open up the home defence, and Borough were disciplined, alert and resilient.

Sources indicate that A night to freeze the breath. A match to warm Borough hearts. And with 22 victories in 24 games, King's men have the momentum, the belief, and that mental force-field to carry them into the deepest of Decembers and out the other side.
